Mr. Speaker, in his speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, as well as in the course of his political campaign in the province of Quebec, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) stressed the difficulties that have arisen in dominion-provincial relations with regard to taxation, but he is wary of suggesting means of arriving at some permanent form of agreement in the matter. In my opinion that shows the irresponsibility of his attitude. I believe that the electors of Quebec have good cause to doubt the sincerity of the Leader of the Opposition and are bound to examine his political past before passing judgment on the matter.
I must say that the political background of a man still is the best way of weighing what he says as a member of the opposition against what he would do should, he ever win an election. In that connection may I be permitted to draw the attention of the house to the following statements of the Leader of the Opposition on provincial autonomy, giving the dates they were uttered, and as reproduced in he Canada of Thursday, September 4, 1952. On February 23, 1935, he said:
If everything had to be done all over again, who would be mad enough to establish in Canada ten governments instead of one?
On November 10, 1936, he said:
Canada must do away with the costly inefficiency of ten governments which, in most cases, do what a single government could accomplish.
On January 26, 1939, he had this to say:
I declare myself in favour of consolidating national ties and depriving the provinces of all powers incompatible with those of the central government, when these powers are not required for the administration of the province.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is the way to say it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
On April 24, 1941, he said:
The integrity of a nation can be safeguarded only through a strong feeling in favour of centralization.
On November 10, 1936, he had this to say:
Canada should remedy the costly ineptitude of ten governments.
The Address-Mr. LaCroix
As for his friendliness towards our compatriots of the province of Quebec, this is what he had to say on November 29, 1936:
I do not think it unfair to remind French-Cana-dians that they belong to a vanquished race.
Again in August, 1944, on the occasion of the plebiscite, he said:
Are we to allow an isolationist province to dominate the destiny of a divided Canada? I hope that every one of you will reply with a resounding "no" which shall be heard in every part of the province of Quebec.
All these remarks were uttered while the Leader of the Opposition was either in power or the leader of his party in Ontario. I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, to the Leader of the Opposition here in this house that whether or not he likes it his political past dogs his footsteps. I believe the province of Quebec to be firmly attached to its motto, "Je me souviens". It certainly is not the present Leader of the Opposition who is capable of solving the problem of fiscal relations with Quebec. I have far more confidence in the ability of the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to arrive at a permanent settlement of this question.
Section 91 of the British North America Act enables the federal government to raise moneys by any form or system of taxation in order to ensure an efficient administration for the promotion of peace and order in this country. On the other hand, section 92 grants to provincial governments the exclusive right to implement direct taxation in the provinces in order to enable them to levy the funds necessary for the administration of their provinces.
On the face of it, it seems that both governments enjoy the same rights of taxation and, to my knowledge, this opinion has never been questioned by our courts, for no provincial government has ever dared to institute proceedings in this regard, probably being convinced in advance that a final ruling would grant the same rights to both governments in this field. In any event I am convinced that, regardless of the government in power, Quebec will never surrender the rights guaranteed to her by section 92, any more than the federal government will surrender those which it claims are guaranteed to it by section 91.
Obviously the fathers of confederation had not foreseen that one day Canada would be a great nation and that we would be involved in international problems demanding tremendous expenses which the beginning of our federal existence could not foreshadow. This is an unfortunate situation, for it is evident that the federal government, like the provincial governments, may embark upon a

The Address-Mr. LaCroix wild rush toward the same fields of taxation, although according to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) himself, they have now reached the extreme point of saturation. Consequently a solution must be found which, without depriving the federal government and the provinces of the privileges they enjoy under the constitution, would ensure their security in the field of revenue, without having to increase the burden on an already overtaxed population.
I believe it would be in everybody's interest to revise and specify as soon as possible the limits of taxation possibilities granted each government; for temporary subsidies, because of vested interests, leave the receiving government at the donor's mercy and produce an entirely inacceptable situation as far as my province is concerned. In view of this, may I be allowed to submit to the government the following solution which, I believe, would have the advantage of abolishing the system of subsidies, which is sure to be considered in time as a final withdrawal of the provinces.
Subsidies could be replaced by a permanent arrangement which would provide, under our constitution, for the annual remittance to each province of a percentage, to be determined, of the total income and corporation taxes collected by Ottawa in that province, while leaving the latter in full control of succession duties. As far as Quebec is concerned, there are special reasons to retain succession duties owing to the close relationship between the requirements of our French civil code and our successions.
According to figures provided by the Department of Finance, the income and corporate taxes in Ontario for the year ending March 31, 1952, yielded a total amount of $998,517,170.22. Under the recent agreement between the federal government and the government of Ontario, providing for withdrawal from these two fields of taxation, the province of Ontario will receive annually a grant of $123,327,363.07. This amounts to a little more than 12 per cent of the total revenue collected in a year by the federal government in Ontario in these two fields of taxation. My information is that the province of Ontario yields the largest amount of income and corporate tax.
An agreement providing for an automatic refund to the province of Quebec of a percentage, to be agreed upon between the central government and the province of Quebec, of the total amount of income and corporate taxes collected annually in Quebec would recognize, I think, the undeniable right of the province to levy direct taxes, would simplify collection, and at the same time

allow for the variations in Canada's economic situation. I believe that in time it would prove to the advantage of both governments, since the federal government would not have to enter into temporary financial agreements which at the end of five years, or perhaps sooner, might seem quite heavy on the budget. Unless both governments come to some permanent agreement one may well expect that, should a depression come about, the two above-mentioned taxes will be applied in a manner that will soon bring about an economic disaster and a real threat to our Canadian economy.
For the people of Quebec an agreement is essential because otherwise corporations will continue to pay to the province of Quebec a 7 per cent tax which, added to the federal tax, makes a total of 54 per cent; while in Ontario and the other provinces that have signed agreements, of a so-called temporary character, corporations will pay one tax only amounting to 52 per cent. Such a state of affairs is bound to be detrimental to Quebec's industrial development, since many large industrial concerns which obtain their raw material from outside Quebec might resolve, in order to avoid paying 2 per cent more on capital and profit, to move their installations to the province of Ontario.
It would also be possible to implement, through an agreement between the two governments, the proposition that a single form for both personal and corporation income tax be set, each government collecting separately the share required under their respective legislation. This would undoubtedly provide the public with an opportunity to understand better the burden laid upon them by each government.
I cannot be reckoned as a political admirer of Mr. Duplessis and my feelings in this connection are well-known. Nevertheless I do believe that Mr. Lapalme, the leader of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, would also welcome an agreement defining once and for all the taxation powers of each government. The pretext of fiscal autonomy must cease to be used as a continuously resorted to political expedient, without the least solution ever being suggested.
Mr. Speaker, I take the liberty from my seat in the House of Commons to make these suggestions, which are not perfect but, nevertheless, deserve to be studied.
The present Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who is most favourably disposed towards my province, will not hold office eternally. We are by no means sure

that his successor, acting under the inspiration of an essentially centralizing bureaucracy, will not adopt as his fiscal mottoes the declarations made by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) on February 23, 1935, November 10, 1936, January 26, 1939, April 24, 1941, and so on. Such an attitude will prevent Quebec from controlling its educational, hospital and other services, services which are our very own, which are guaranteed by the constitution, which are essential to the maintenance and development of a French and Catholic culture which in turn provides this whole country with a really invaluable intellectual asset.
The Right Hon. Prime Minister has already made many efforts to arrive at an agreement in this matter. I believe there should be a solution. If the Right Hon. Prime Minister and the premier of Quebec could manage to save our federal system of government, whatever the effort, they would be doing this country immense service. In a land as rich and diversified as ours, it is the only system compatible with true democracy.

Just yesterday the member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) said that a great event was taking place in Toronto tomorrow, a football game. Both the candidates for mayor have said that they are running on a ticket for higher federal grants. I believe it is time, Mr. Speaker, that someone said something in this house about these grants. In Canada we have a constitution, the British North America Act. In that act it is stated that no government shall pay taxes. The city of Ottawa is claiming that grants should be paid to the city from the federal treasury for the services that are being rendered to the people of Canada. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada are rendering a service to this city. Why should the people of Ottawa ask the people of Canada to help them pay their taxes?
The Address-Mr. Ferrie
Today between 38,000 and 40,000 people in the city of Ottawa are working for the people of Canada. If it were not for the buildings that are here, if it were not for the fact the government is here, would there be such a place as Ottawa? Many years ago it was known as Bytown, and it would still be known as Bytown if it had not been chosen as the capital city. I want to say that if the government is going to give this grant to the city of Ottawa, then let them give grants to the 4,200 other municipalities in the Dominion of Canada. The municipalities in the western provinces are just as much entitled to those grants as the city of Ottawa. These two candidates have appeared on the platform and asked the people of Ottawa to elect one of them as mayor of this city, but both say that they want higher federal grants. When the estimate covering this grant comes up I, for one, am going to propose that it be cut to $1. I am sure that the people of Canada would be well satisfied to see these grants reduced. These people in the city of Ottawa are just as much entitled to pay taxes for improvements as anyone else in any other part of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO LEGISLATION TO PERMIT GARNISHEEING OF WAGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief statement with regard to a matter concerning which I think a good deal of misunderstanding will arise if it is not corrected promptly.

subtopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO LEGISLATION TO PERMIT GARNISHEEING OF WAGES
speechtext:
What is the nature of the statement? What is the subject matter? If we
are told that, we can indicate whether or not we agree to the statement being made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO LEGISLATION TO PERMIT GARNISHEEING OF WAGES
speechtext:
The subject matter is a story in this evening's Citizen to this effect:
The garnisheeing of wages of federal government employees is expected to be permitted under legislation which may be introduced at the current session of parliament, it was learned today.
I think it would create a great deal of misunderstanding if a story like that went out. I may say that there is no foundation for that story. There is no intention to introduce any such legislation. The reference in the speech from the throne which is quoted in this newspaper article to this effect-and I am now quoting from the reference in the newspaper-
... A measure will be submitted designed to place the crown in substantially the same position as a private person with respect to liability for acts committed by its servants.
-is only partially quoted. The full text of that selection from the speech from the throne goes on in the speech itself as follows: . . . for breach of duty arising out of the ownership or occupation of property, and for salvage claims . . .
Exposing the crown to suit for the acts of its servants in connection with breach of duty arising out of the ownership or occupation of property has nothing to do with the garnishee process at all, and it is not the intention of the government to introduce legislation permitting the garnisheeing of civil service wages.
